name: Long face syndrome theory

card.summary: The idea that long-term mouth breathing lengthens and narrows the face, used by people to decide whether to work on nasal breathing, posture and jaw or midface treatment to improve facial proportions.
card.aka: Adenoid face, adenoid facies, long face, rhinitis face
card.note: Orthodontic literature treats the link between breathing mode and face shape as debated, and individual responses vary.

quick.overview:
Long face syndrome is an orthodontic term for a face with increased lower facial height, often with a narrow upper jaw, an open-mouth posture and a steep jaw angle. The "theory" is the proposal that long-term mouth breathing, for example from enlarged adenoids or chronic nasal obstruction, drives this growth pattern in children.

For appearance, the theory points to a concrete chain: restore nasal breathing in childhood, lip seal and tongue posture follow, and facial growth may be steered toward a shorter, broader face. In adults, long-face traits are addressed with orthodontics, jaw surgery or chin procedures. Reviews describe the breathing link as supported by some studies and contested by others.
quick.how: In practice people look at it in three ways. Parents and clinicians check children for chronic mouth breathing and have enlarged adenoids or rhinitis assessed by an ear, nose and throat specialist. Orthodontists may use early appliances or myofunctional approaches during growth. Adults in looksmaxxing forums compare face-length ratios, discuss nasal breathing and tongue posture, and ask about bimaxillary surgery, genioplasty, hairstyles and beards that change how the lower face reads.
quick.risks: The condition itself is a growth pattern rather than a disease, but the underlying airway obstruction can be linked to sleep-disordered breathing and ear problems, so clinicians evaluate it. Treatments carry their own risks: adenoidectomy and jaw surgery are operations with anaesthesia and recovery periods, and orthodontic reviews note that long-face patients can be more difficult to treat. Responses to changed breathing in human studies vary widely between individuals.

lead: Long face syndrome, also called adenoid face or adenoid facies, is a term from orthodontics and maxillofacial surgery for a vertical facial growth pattern: increased lower anterior face height, a narrow upper dental arch, a steep mandibular plane, lip incompetence (lips that do not rest together), often a gummy smile and, in many descriptions, a retruded chin.[1][2][3][22] The long face syndrome theory is the proposal that chronic mouth breathing during childhood, usually from enlarged adenoids or persistent nasal obstruction, causes or contributes to this pattern.[3][4][24]

The theory matters to people interested in appearance because it links face shape to things that can be addressed: the nasal airway in childhood, tongue and lip posture, and in adulthood orthodontic-surgical treatment, chin procedures, hairstyles and facial hair. Looksmaxxing forum members discuss it alongside mewing, midface projection and bimaxillary ("bimax") surgery, and use it to explain why some faces look longer and narrower than others.[5][6][37] Adults with a skeletal long-face pattern are described in the clinical literature as candidates for combined orthodontic and jaw surgery such as Le Fort I maxillary impaction.[7][26]

Research on the breathing link spans decades. Experimental work in animals suggested that switching to mouth breathing changes muscle function and increases vertical face growth, while human studies have been more mixed, and reviewers have said individual variation should be expected.[4][8] Wikipedia notes that both the diagnosis and the status of long face as a true "syndrome" are disputed, and that genetic and environmental causes are both proposed.[22] Recent reviews of rhinitis-related adenoid facies continue to describe characteristic features and propose multidisciplinary management.[9]

chain: Nasal obstruction or enlarged adenoids in childhood
Habitual mouth breathing and altered tongue and lip posture
Proposed increase in lower face height and narrower jaw
Earlier airway treatment or later orthodontic and surgical work to rebalance the face
angle.text: The theory gives people a framework for understanding a long, narrow lower face and for deciding when to look at airway health, orthodontics or jaw surgery. In adults, the practical routes described in the literature are orthodontic-surgical corrections and chin or hair and beard styling choices.

paras: Clinical descriptions list an open-mouth posture with the tongue tip visible, a long lower face, midface narrowness, a high-arched palate, proclined upper incisors and open bite as typical features of adenoid facies.[1][2] Rhinitis-related versions can also include periorbital signs such as allergic shiners (dark circles under the eyes) and Dennie-Morgan lines (infraorbital folds associated with atopy), and a horizontal nasal crease from repeated nose rubbing.[9]

The orthodontic description of the skeletal version comes from a 1976 paper by Schendel and colleagues, who analysed 31 adults with a clinically recognisable long-face morphology. They reported that the deformity is associated with excessive vertical growth of the maxilla and described dental open bite and closed bite as two variants.[10][22] Grokipedia and other summaries list a gummy smile, an elongated philtrum, a thin upper lip, a convex profile with a recessed chin and a narrow nasal base among the common features, noting that not every person has all of them.[3]

Orthodontic writing has also used the term for a skeletal pattern called vertical maxillary excess, in which the upper jaw is vertically long, with or without any history of mouth breathing.[10][11] A cephalometric measurement called the MM angle has been proposed to help diagnose the pattern, and clinicians describe vertical control as one of the more difficult parts of orthodontic therapy.[12] Biomechanical modelling of the temporalis and masseter muscles has compared long-face and short-face patients and found that differences in face shape change the mechanical advantage of the jaw muscles.[28] A comparison of hyoid bone position in 39 adults with long face syndrome and open bite against 43 adults with normal occlusion examined how the tongue-bone complex sits in this morphology.[31]

Wikipedia's article on the topic adds that the term overlaps with skeletal open bite and that some surgeons, including the pioneering jaw surgeon Hugo Obwegeser, have argued that its signs do not meet the threshold for a syndrome in the strict medical sense.[22] In practice the phrase is used loosely online to mean any face with a long lower third.

The link between a blocked nose and a changed face is older than orthodontics. In 1868 the Danish physician Hans Wilhelm Meyer described adenoid vegetations and tied them to mouth breathing, snoring and hearing loss, and by the early twentieth century physicians were describing a typical "mouth-breather" face.[15][24] The term adenoid facies grew out of that tradition and still appears in current ENT guidelines.[1][15]

The vocabulary of "long face syndrome" was formalised in the 1970s. Schendel's 1976 description was followed by 1977 reports on surgical correction, including Le Fort I osteotomy modifications and a companion paper on surgical correction of the syndrome, and by a 1978 cephalometric study of rotation patterns in long-face and short-face subjects.[7][10][11][17] Reviews in the early 1980s then examined how nasal respiration relates to dentofacial form, and a 1986 review discussed nasal respiratory function and craniofacial growth.[18][29][30]

A 1990 review in The Angle Orthodontist, titled for the long face syndrome and impairment of the nasopharyngeal airway, summarised the position that had emerged: experimental evidence suggests that a switch from nasal to oronasal breathing produces functional adaptations including increased anterior face height, and animal studies had suggested predictable growth patterns, while human studies had been much more controversial.[4] Wikipedia credits this line of work to the University of Minnesota researcher Luc Tourne.[22]

The hypothesis holds that blocked nasal airflow changes head posture, tongue position and muscle balance, which in turn directs growth of the jaws downward and backward during childhood.[4][8] Reviews summarise animal experiments that support this and note that after adenoidectomy, some children show accelerated mandibular growth, which has been used as supporting evidence.[8]

Human studies have been more controversial. A 1990 review concluded that individual variations in response should be expected when breathing mode changes.[4] A 2007 review revisiting the question reported that the original proposals have been debated for decades.[8] A 2025 Chinese review of early orthodontic treatment addresses whether early intervention can treat habitual mouth breathing or adenoid face as one of several questions on which expectations may be exaggerated.[13]

Wikipedia's article on mouth breathing says that chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and may lead to a long, narrow face, and it also records the reverse possibility: that a long, thin face with a narrow airway may predispose a person to nasal obstruction and mouth breathing.[24] The same article notes that research on the health effects of mouth breathing sits across orthodontics, myofunctional therapy and anthropology, and that mouth taping has been little studied.[24]

Proponents of the causal view point to the mechanism (airway first, posture second, growth third), to children whose faces change after adenoid surgery and to the consistent clinical appearance of adenoid facies.[2][8] Researchers who question it point to the high heritability of vertical facial dimensions reported in the literature, to the large individual variation in human responses and to the fact that a long face can exist without any history of nasal obstruction.[3][4][10]

Clinicians do not look at the long face in isolation. Adenoid enlargement is associated with eustachian tube dysfunction, recurrent middle-ear infection, snoring and disturbed sleep, and the German S2k guideline directs examiners to look for adenoid facies, with a permanently open mouth and visible tongue tip, during assessment.[1][14] Wikipedia notes that long face syndrome is sometimes associated with paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea and allergies and that physicians should distinguish these conditions.[22]

Case reports describe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with long face syndrome, with polysomnography and cephalometry used to locate the site of obstruction.[32] Because the airway and the jaw are anatomically linked, orthognathic surgeons also note that jaw advancement and repositioning are used to treat obstructive sleep apnoea in some patients.[26]

The 2023 German S2k guideline on adenoid hypertrophy states that examiners should look for adenoid facies and that adenoidectomy is the usual procedure when symptoms are severe or conservative treatment fails.[1][14] The Wikipedia summary of adenoid hypertrophy also notes that watchful waiting and intranasal corticosteroids are used for milder cases, and that the adenoid normally enlarges between roughly ages 6 and 10 and shrinks by around 16.[15]

In growing children, Wikipedia describes the aim of treatment as halting and controlling downward growth of the lower jaw and limiting further eruption of the back teeth, and that in severe cases orthodontics combined with jaw surgery may be the only effective option.[22] Orthodontic reviews describe treatment options intended to limit vertical expression during growth.[12] Recent case reports describe mini-implant approaches and combined therapy for hyperdivergent growing patients.[3]

For established skeletal long-face patterns, case series from the 1970s onward describe Le Fort I osteotomy to reduce vertical height combined with orthodontics, and genioplasty procedures to address chin vertical excess.[7][16][36] A 2016 French review and a 1989 Canadian overview of orthodontics list long-face syndrome among the situations in which orthodontic-surgical treatment is considered.[33][34] Wikipedia's article on orthognathic surgery describes a total maxillary osteotomy as the operation used for vertical maxillary excess and gives typical recovery as two to six weeks of initial healing followed by two to four months of bone remodelling, with swelling lasting a few months.[26]

Outside surgery, people with a long face use non-surgical routes aimed at changing how the face reads. Chin augmentation, including quick implant techniques, can add projection to a recessed chin, and surgeons have described "functional" genioplasty as a way of shortening an excessive chin height.[16][35][36] Hairstyles with width or fringe, and beards that add fullness at the sides of the jaw, are discussed in forums as ways to alter apparent face length.[20][21]

Published work includes the 1976 clinical and cephalometric analysis of 31 adults,[10] cephalometric comparisons of long-face and short-face adults and of rotation patterns,[17] biomechanical modelling of the jaw muscles,[28] comparison of hyoid position in adults with long face and open bite versus normal occlusion,[31] reviews of nasal respiration and craniofacial growth,[8][18][29][30] and surgical case reports on Le Fort I correction.[7][11] A 1977 report of Le Fort I osteotomy described the combined orthodontic and surgical plan used to reduce facial height and align the bite.[7]

The strength of the evidence for mouth breathing as the cause is described by reviewers as variable between individuals: animal studies support a causal mechanism, human studies are more mixed, and the 1990 and 2007 reviews both state this.[4][8] A 2025 review of rhinitis-induced adenoid facies in children and adolescents describes the clinical features, the proposed pathophysiology and a multidisciplinary management approach.[2][9]

On looksmax.org, threads ask whether bimaxillary surgery corrects a long face, which hairstyles suit a long face and big forehead, and whether beards can even out a long face.[19][20][21] A thread on a long face and midface asks about counter-clockwise bimax rotation and other options, with replies noting that maxillary impaction can shorten the philtrum; another on a long face or skull asks about surgery and implants, with replies saying that a bimax can widen the jaw and chin but may help less if there is no gummy smile.[37][38]

Others speculate about the causes of an adenoid face in their own photos, often tying it to childhood nasal breathing.[6] Some members ask whether growth hormone would lengthen a long lower third, and replies in those threads describe the outcome as dependent on genetics.[5] The concept sits near mewing and mouth taping in forum conversation: Wikipedia describes mewing, the oral posture practice associated with the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, as a form of posture training that claims to guide jaw and facial development, and records that the American Association of Orthodontists and most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to orthognathic surgery.[23][25] John Mew's orthotropic proposal that malocclusion is a postural deformity dates from 1958, and Wikipedia reports that he visited Rolf Fränkel in East Germany in 1968.[23]

Wikipedia's article on long face syndrome notes the actor and screenwriter Craig Chester, who has written about living with the condition.[22] Public interest in jaw and face shape rose sharply in 2019 according to Google Trends, which Wikipedia links to social media virality in looksmaxxing communities.[25]

timeline.event: Danish physician Hans Wilhelm Meyer describes adenoid vegetations and links them to mouth breathing, snoring and hearing loss.[15]
John Mew proposes the "Tropic Premise", arguing malocclusion is a postural deformity, a root of later orthotropic and mewing ideas.[23]
Schendel and colleagues describe the long face syndrome as vertical maxillary excess in 31 adults.[10]
Reports describe Le Fort I osteotomy modifications and surgical correction of the long face syndrome.[7][11]
Papers on mode of respiration and facial growth and on jaw-muscle biomechanics in long-face and short-face patients appear in the American Journal of Orthodontics.[28][29]
A review in Archives of Otolaryngology discusses nasal respiratory function and craniofacial growth.[18]
A review concludes human responses to altered breathing vary individually.[4]
A European Journal of Orthodontics review revisits the effect of breathing mode on craniofacial growth.[8]
Interest in mewing and jaw structure surges online, according to Google Trends.[25]
The German S2k adenoid guideline lists adenoid facies as an examination finding.[1]
A Frontiers in Allergy review describes rhinitis-induced adenoid facies in children.[9]

lore.intro: Forum members use the term for a long lower face and attribute it to childhood mouth breathing, then compare surgical and non-surgical ways to change it.[6][19]

claims.claim: Childhood mouth breathing lengthened my face
claims.believers: Posters describing an adenoid face argue that chronic nasal obstruction shaped their facial growth and point to open-mouth posture and a narrow maxilla.[6]
claims.experts: Reviews describe a plausible mechanism and animal support, while human studies are described as more controversial with individual variation.[4][8]

claims.claim: Jaw surgery can correct a long face
claims.believers: Users ask whether bimaxillary surgery fixes the pattern and discuss maxillary impaction as the route.[19][37]
claims.experts: Surgical reports describe Le Fort I osteotomy combined with orthodontics to reduce facial height.[7][26]

claims.claim: Bimax only helps if there is a gummy smile
claims.believers: A reply in one thread says bimax will not always help a long face if there is no gummy smile, while another says it can also widen the jaw and chin.[38]
claims.experts: Surgical literature describes the plan as individualised to the dentofacial deformity, bite and aesthetics.[7]

claims.claim: Hairstyles and beards can visually balance a long face
claims.believers: Threads discuss styling choices intended to shorten the apparent length of the face.[20][21]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested styling as a way of changing perceived face length.

claims.claim: Mewing or tongue posture can shorten or widen a long face
claims.believers: Mewing advocates say correct tongue posture and lip seal guide facial growth toward a broader, shorter shape.[25]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that no credible scientific research has proven orthotropics effective and that the American Association of Orthodontists sees no evidence it improves the jaw; a 2019 review found some plausible conclusions but inadequate efficacy evidence.[23][25]

claims.claim: Growth hormone will make a long face longer
claims.believers: Teens in forum threads worry that growth hormone would extend a long lower third and ask whether it would grow longer or wider.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies in the orthodontic long-face literature have tested this question; replies in the forum itself say the result would depend on genetics.[5]

claims.believers: Some people describe the pattern as inherited and correctable only by extensive surgery.[22]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and reviews describe both genetic and environmental causes, with experts disagreeing about how they interact; heritability estimates for facial height are reported as high.[3][22]

claims.claim: Treating adenoids early can change facial growth
claims.believers: Parents and clinicians point to children whose mandibular growth accelerated after adenoidectomy as support for early airway treatment.[8]
claims.experts: The 2023 guideline recommends adenoidectomy for symptom control when conservative treatment fails and does not set facial shape as the indication; a 2025 review questions what early intervention can promise.[1][13]
